Mixed media work by Komakula Raja Sekhar | Photo Credit: SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT
In artist Komakula Raja Sekhar’s world, there is no dearth of colour.
His mixed-media works bring to life a colourful neighbourhood where animals, particularly elephants, goats and peacocks, step out of their natural habitats and inhabit an imaginative world.
Born and raised in Narsipatnam, near Visakhapatnam, and now based in Hyderabad, Komakula draws much of his inspiration from the villages he grew up around. His paintings capture fragments of that familiar landscape, offering visitors a glimpse into his world at his ongoing solo exhibition at Art Space by Kalpadruma.
Mixed media work by Komakula Raja Sekhar | Photo Credit: SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT
Made with pencils, ink pens and watercolours on acid-free paper, the works share a familiar visual language. From a distance, the colourful houses and trees look like different views of the same neighbourhood. Once you peek closer, they reveal subtle variations, particularly in the animals that inhabit these scenes. While some compositions feature elephants alongside goats, others have peacocks at the centre, making it a recurring motif.
Roosters also appear frequently around the houses. As Komakula explains, “In most of these village houses, the families own roosters and goats.”
The houses here are in bright shades of blue, red, orange, violet, and yellow. The attention to detail also extends to the windows, with no two windows looking alike. The variations, Komakula says, are a distinct characteristic of these houses.
The trees and flowers are inspired by Indian miniatures | Photo Credit: SPECIAL ARRANGEMENT
Apart from the houses, trees and flowers also play an important role in the paintings. The trees and flowers that branch out in the middle of the houses, the artist says, are inspired by Indian miniatures (a style of painting that became famous during the Mughal era). “Because of the detailing, some of these paintings can take almost 40 days to finish.”
Komakula is trained in graphics at Andhra University and completed his Master's at Kala Bhavan, Visva-Bharati, Santiniketan. After completing his Master’s, he returned to Hyderabad, where he worked with artists Sumanto Chowdhury and Laxma Goud. “I have been particularly influenced by Laxma Goud’s black-and-white paintings,” he says.
Growing up, Komakula never thought of taking up painting as a profession. Like any other kid, he was just happy drawing cartoons. “Sometimes I used to sit beside my uncle and paint. Since he is also a painter, he used to tell me that I should think of taking up painting later,” says Komakula.
The exhibition also features some of his black-and-white etchings and aquatints, techniques he says he learned during his college years.
While most of his paintings are filled with Nature and animals, human figures are conspicuously absent. Asked if this was a deliberate choice, he smiles and says, “maybe next time I will paint humans.”
Komakula Raja Sekhar’s solo exhibition is currently on at Art Space by Kalpadruma, 37, Gopalapuram 1st Street, till November 21. Entry open for all.
